record.original_question: What fundamental principle, beyond general covariance and the equivalence principle for geodesic motion, uniquely selects the Einstein-Hilbert action and the second-order Einstein field equations as the necessary classical gravitational dynamics? General covariance establishes that gravity can be formulated as a metric-based field theory, but by itself it does not determine which covariant scalar action should govern the metric.

evidence.quote: The standard theory thus still awaits the identification of some principle which would then make it necessary too.

the loose ends which we discuss below not only need to be tidied up, but that they need to be resolved in favor of the standard theory by the identifying of some currently unknown fundamental principle which would then ensure that the standard theory in fact be a necessary and not merely a sufficient theory of gravity.

Thus the question of what (covariant) equation of motion is to fix the Christoffel symbols which are to go into Eq. (9) is in principle an independently explorable issue which is decoupled from the validity or otherwise of the equivalence principle, and constitutes the only piece of the entire Einstein package which would still appear to admit of further analysis.

Thus while it can safely be said that gravity is indeed a metric based field theory, covariance alone is simply not sufficient to specify the gravitational action with more input being needed, since any covariant scalar action whatsoever will meet that requirement.

Now in a sense it is quite remarkable that Einstein did not appeal to something like a fundamental principle which would then unambiguously specify the appropriate action, since that would be more in keeping with the viewpoint which motivated his explanation of the equality of gravitational and inertial masses.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider classical gravity formulated as a metric field theory on a four-dimensional Lorentzian manifold, in which the dynamical variable is a metric tensor $g_{\mu\nu}$ and the field equations are derived from a generally covariant scalar action $S[g]=\int \mathcal{L}(g_{\mu\nu},\partial g,\partial^2 g,\ldots)\sqrt{-g}\,d^4x$. Assume:

(i) General covariance (diffeomorphism invariance of the action), so that gravity is a metric-based field theory.

(ii) The equivalence principle for geodesic motion, i.e., free test particles follow geodesics of the metric connection.

These two assumptions alone do not single out a particular Lagrangian, since any generally covariant scalar functional of the metric and its derivatives is compatible with them.

Problem. Identify and rigorously formulate an additional fundamental physical or mathematical principle, independent of (i) and (ii), with the property that the combination of (i), (ii), and this new principle necessarily selects the Einstein–Hilbert Lagrangian $\mathcal{L}_{EH}=\tfrac{1}{2\kappa}(R-2\Lambda)$ (and hence the second-order Einstein field equations $G_{\mu\nu}+\Lambda g_{\mu\nu}=\kappa T_{\mu\nu}$) as the unique classical gravitational dynamics in four spacetime dimensions, making the standard theory not merely sufficient but necessary.
artifact.status_search_result: Lovelock's theorem (1971) shows that in four dimensions, requiring the field equations to be derived from a metric Lagrangian and to be of at most second order in derivatives, divergence-free, and symmetric uniquely selects the Einstein tensor (plus cosmological constant). This is widely regarded as a partial answer: it pinpoints "second-order equations of motion" as a uniqueness criterion, but does not by itself give a deeper physical principle making this restriction necessary. Modern variants (e.g., dimensional/stress-energy arguments, consistent Levi-Civita truncations) refine the criterion. No single universally accepted "fundamental principle" beyond such technical assumptions has emerged, so the foundational question remains open in the philosophical/physical sense while being partially addressed mathematically.

status_evidence.title: Lovelock's theorem - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: From a local gravitational action containing only second derivatives of the four-dimensional spacetime metric, the only possible equations of motion are the Einstein field equations.
status_evidence.claim: Lovelock's theorem gives a uniqueness result for the Einstein equations under the second-order assumption in 4D.

status_evidence.title: A Simple Proof of the Uniqueness of the Einstein Field Equation in All Dimensions
status_evidence.snippet: Modified Lovelock's assumption to require that the curvature tensor have the physical dimension of stress-energy, yielding uniqueness in all dimensions.
status_evidence.claim: Recent work refines uniqueness criteria for the Einstein field equations beyond Lovelock's original assumptions.
